analysis.one_liner: Eliminates the federal law that shields websites from lawsuits over content their users post.
analysis.headline: Introduced December 17, 2025 by ten senators from both parties and referred to the Senate Commerce Committee, where it sat without a hearing or vote as the year ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Section 230 of the Communications Act of 1934 is the rule that says a website is generally not legally responsible for what its users post — it is why social media sites, comment sections, forums, and reviews can exist. This bill wipes that protection out entirely, along with every reference to it in other federal laws, starting two years after it is enacted. After that, anyone who believes they were harmed by something posted online could sue the platform that hosted it, not just the person who posted it. The bill does not replace Section 230 with anything; it simply ends it.
analysis.who_benefits: People harmed by online content — victims of defamation, fraud, harassment, nonconsensual images, drug sales, or exploitation that platforms decline to remove — would gain the right to sue the platform that hosted the material, not just the anonymous poster. Plaintiffs' attorneys would gain a large new field of litigation. Whoever wins those suits could recover damages from companies that today are legally untouchable.

how_it_helps.text: Restores the ability to sue the website itself over defamatory, fraudulent, or unlawful content posted by users, instead of being limited to suing the anonymous poster.
The repeal takes effect two years after enactment, giving platforms and courts time to adjust before the immunity disappears.
Rewrites roughly a dozen other federal laws that reference Section 230 so that its removal does not leave those statutes in limbo.

analysis.who_pays: Internet platforms large and small bear the cost: they would face lawsuits over user posts and would likely respond by removing far more content, shutting down comment sections, forums, and reviews, or blocking users from certain regions to limit exposure. Small websites and nonprofits without legal departments would be hit hardest, and users would bear the cost of a thinner, more heavily filtered internet.
analysis.who_pays_short: Websites big and small, and internet users

drawbacks.text: The bill repeals Section 230 outright rather than reforming it, with no replacement framework for content moderation, so platforms would have to choose between unlimited moderation and unlimited legal exposure.

The immunity being repealed covers not just large social media companies but every website, blog host, mailing list, and forum that carries third-party content, including small sites, nonprofits, and libraries, which would face the same lawsuit exposure as the biggest platforms.

Facing lawsuits over virtually any user post, platforms would likely remove large amounts of lawful speech and could shut down comment sections, user forums, and review features entirely, leaving ordinary users with fewer places to speak online.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The case for the bill is real: Section 230 can leave people with no recourse when a platform hosts defamatory lies, revenge porn, or illegal sales, because the site itself cannot be sued. But the bill takes the bluntest possible route — a total repeal with no replacement framework — rather than narrowing the law to target specific harms. Repeal would sweep in small websites, nonprofit forums, and everyday users who forward or host content, exposing them to litigation they cannot afford, and platforms would likely respond by removing huge amounts of lawful speech to avoid being dragged into court. An honest supporter would acknowledge that the bill trades one set of harms (platforms escaping accountability) for another (a more litigious, more censored, thinner internet), without any transition plan beyond a two-year delay.

outcome.mechanism: It was just introduced and sent to committee, and it has not had a hearing, a vote, or any further action since.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced in the Senate on December 17, 2025.
It was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation the same day, its only action so far.
The bill was introduced by Senator Lindsey Graham together with nine other senators from both parties, including Dick Durbin, Chuck Grassley, Amy Klobuchar, and Josh Hawley.

The bill's single substantive section repeals Section 230 of the Communications Act of 1934, the law that keeps websites from being treated as the publisher of what their users post, effective two years after enactment.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, no one has gained or lost anything: the bill has only been referred to committee. If it never advances, the largest internet platforms keep the liability shield they have operated under since 1996.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one yet; bill sits in committee

for.name: Sen. Lindsey Graham
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill in the Senate on December 17, 2025.

for.name: Nine bipartisan co-introducers
for.role: Senators Durbin, Grassley, Whitehouse, Hawley, Klobuchar, Blackburn, Blumenthal, Moody, and Welch
for.what_they_did: Joined as original cosponsors, giving the bill 5 Democrats and 4 Republicans alongside its Republican sponsor.

against.name: Major internet platforms and tech industry groups
against.what_they_did: Have long opposed any repeal of Section 230, the legal foundation of the user-generated internet, and can be expected to fight this bill.

sides.party_line_note: The ten sponsors split evenly across party lines — 5 Democrats and 5 Republicans — an unusual alliance of senators who otherwise disagree on most things but share frustration with social media companies.

industries.industry: Social media platforms and large internet companies
industries.note: Repeal strips away the legal shield that has protected them from being sued over user-posted content since 1996, exposing them to defamation, negligence, and product-liability suits. Users would likely see more content removed and fewer interactive features as platforms try to limit risk.

industries.industry: Small websites, forums, blogs, and nonprofits hosting third-party content
industries.note: Section 230 protects every site that carries user content, not just billion-dollar companies; without it, small operators face the same lawsuit risk as the giants and many would shut down comment sections, forums, or hosting entirely. Their interest in keeping the shield runs alongside the public's interest in an open, diverse internet.

Repeal opens a vast new body of potential lawsuits against websites for their users' posts. Some of those suits would compensate genuinely injured people, while others would target lawful speech and small defendants.

analysis.trajectory: This Congress is still in session. A full repeal of Section 230 has never advanced out of committee, and the bill received no committee action in the weeks after its introduction. Its bipartisan sponsorship makes a hearing possible, but replacing a foundation of the modern internet without any substitute framework is a heavy lift; the realistic path is that it sits in the Commerce Committee like previous repeal attempts, possibly resurfacing as part of a broader online-harms or child-safety bill that narrows Section 230 instead of ending it.
